column12: Customer outage time after a failure, from EAGLE-I Davidson County 2015–2025 excl. 2018 (scripts/eaglei_restoration.py → twin/evidence/eaglei_restoration.json). Non-storm events with peak > 3,000 customers and ≥ 30 min (n = 278): duration q25/q50/q75/q90 = 0.75/1.38/2.75/5.25 h; storm events (n = 269) q50/q90 = 3.0/12.8 h. Low/mid follow the non-storm quantiles; high covers storm-like or equipment-replacement cases. Includes restoration by switching, so it is customer outage time, not equipment repair time. Previous placeholder 4/8/24 h.
column16: Reproducible analysis of local EAGLE-I data (scripts/eaglei_restoration.py); customer restoration, not repair. Corroborated by NES CAIDI without major events, 68–86 min in 2015–2024 (EIA-861).

column12: Required by CMS (81 FR 63860). Diesel failure to start 0.13% (well maintained) to 1.65% (poorly maintained) (Marqusee & Jenket 2020, Tables 2–4). Hurricane Maria: 57 of 64 hospitals (89%) had an operable generator (Irvin-Barnwell et al. 2020). Japan 2011: generators failed at 12 of 213 hospitals, about 5.6% (secondary, via Klinger et al. 2014). Sandy: 28 of 69 hospitals with utility outages had unreliable backup (41%, flood-driven; HHS OIG 2014 p. 13), not used for heat. Low lowered from 0.02 to 0.01 (failure to start alone is 0.1–1.7%).
column16: Generator reliability (NREL) and disaster surveys; Japan figure secondary.

column12: Defined as the probability that a nursing home in an outage zone cannot maintain cooling. HHS OIG A-02-23-01022 (2026): 72 of 100 sampled homes had emergency-power deficiencies (73% nationally); 53% inadequate maintenance, 39% inadequate circuit coverage. Tennessee rule 0720-18-.14 requires generators for life-sustaining equipment with 24 h of fuel but not for cooling. No measured failure-on-demand rate found; range unchanged (still an assumption for the cooling share).
column16: No measured rate; inferred from the OIG deficiency share and Tennessee rules. CMS sets no rule that generators carry air conditioning (CMS emergency preparedness FAQ).

column12: Dialysis depends on power and water; Kelman et al. (2015) document disrupted dialysis care and excess deaths after Hurricane Sandy. No backup assumed (placeholder for facility-level data).
column16: Kelman et al. 2015 and CMS rule (no generator mandate for dialysis).

column12: 'During the blackout, mortality increased for … nonaccidental (ie, disease-related) deaths (25% [12%-41%])' (Anderson & Bell 2012). Reported for context; not applied to a mortality baseline in v0.
column16: Anderson & Bell 2012 (New York); context only.

column12: 'the concurrence of a multiday blackout event with heat wave conditions to more than double the estimated rate of heat-related mortality' (Stone et al. 2023). Lower bound used as a context factor only.

column12: Facilities lose water only when every production source is down and storage is exhausted. Hydraulics are not modelled in v0 (a WNTR-type model, Klise et al. 2017, is the intended upgrade).
column16: All plants assumed to supply every facility; no hydraulic network.

column12: Probability that a treatment plant cannot run at needed capacity after losing utility power. Omohundro: four 2.5 MW generators for the full 90 MGD; Harrington: four 1,750 kW generators for 72 of 90 MGD (Metro Water Services FY2024 disclosure p. 6). Single-unit failure to start 0.13–1.65% (Marqusee & Jenket 2020, Tables 2–4); with four units the residual risk is common-mode (fuel, switchgear) and Harrington's 20% shortfall. Booster stations not covered. Previous placeholder 0.05/0.15/0.30.
column16: Judgement combining local generator counts with NREL failure rates.

column12: Storage ÷ hourly demand (own calculation). In-service storage 51.7 MG in FY2024 (MWS disclosure, Facts in Brief; the 98.3 MG narrative figure was a drafting inconsistency, resolved with the MWS commercial-paper memorandum, Dec 2025, App. B), about 84 MG once the rebuilt 8th Ave reservoir is fully in service. Demand 109.5 MGD average, 137.8 MGD maximum day → 9.0–11.3 h gross at 51.7 MG, 14.6–18.4 h at 84 MG. Low end assumes about half the storage is usable (fire reserve, pressure; assumption). Previous range 6/12/24 h.
column16: Own calculation from official storage and demand figures (conflict resolved 2026-11-10); usable share assumed. Range 5 / 10 / 18 h adopted 2026-11-10.

column12: Share of signals without working battery backup. Weakest source in the set; NDOT inventory needed. Previous placeholder 0.50/0.75/1.00.

column12: Share of TVA operable summer capacity (38,472 MW in EIA-860 2022) available at peak. NERC Summer Reliability Assessments 2022–2026, SERC-Central risk-scenario table: anticipated vs typical-outage reserve margins give (1 + typical)/(1 + anticipated) = 0.924–0.958 (own calculation). Low end: Winter Storm Elliott, ~7,300 MW unavailable ≈ 0.81 (TVA FY2023 10-K). Mode set below 0.92 for heat derates. SERC-Central is larger than TVA. TVA did not shed load in summers 2015–2025. Previous placeholder 0.82/0.88/0.93.

EIA-930 TVA, June–September 2016–2025: net import at the annual peak hour 194–5,716 MW, 4,282 (2023), 5,716 (2024), 5,067 (2025); top 1% demand hours p5/p50/p95 = 157/2,797/5,124 MW (own analysis, net import = −adjusted total interchange). column12: Capacity of a signalised link when its signal is dark, treated as an all-way stop. All-way-stop practical capacity ~500 veh/h/lane vs 1,750 veh/h of green per lane signalised (French 1956, pp. 22, 27–28); HCM all-way-stop approach capacity 525–1,100 veh/h (Kyte et al. 1994, p. 111); measured single-lane all-way-stop totals 400–1,400 veh/h (Al-Kaisy & Doruk 2023). Own ratio: 500 / (1,750 × 0.45 green) ≈ 0.6 at simple crossings, 0.35–0.45 on multilane arterials. Previous placeholder 0.40/0.50/0.70.

column12: Thermal time constant of a home that loses cooling. No published first-order τ fitted to summer outage data. Simulated outages show a large first-hour jump: Houston 2000s single-family home reaches heat index 33 °C 12 h after a midnight outage (Wijesuriya et al. 2024, Fig. 7); Florida nursing home rises 24 → ~28 °C in 1–2 h (Sun et al. 2020, Fig. 4, read from figure). Fit to the damping in Leigh et al. 2014 Fig. 4 gives τ ≈ 6–12 h (own fit). High value stands in for heavy masonry or sealed homes. Previous placeholder 5/15/40 h.
column16: No fitted time constant published; values read from simulation figures elsewhere.

column12: Indoor equilibrium lift above outdoor air from internal and solar gains, 08:00–20:00 local; 1 K at night (fixed). Closed-window simulations show daily-mean lifts of ~2–5 K and night lifts of ~5–7 K (Sun et al. 2020 Figs. 4, 12; Leigh et al. 2014 Fig. 4; read from figures). The fixed 1 K night lift is likely too small; making it a parameter is planned. Previous placeholder 1/3/6 K.
column16: Values read from simulation figures elsewhere.

column12: Indoor temperature held by a powered air conditioner. RECS 2020 Table HC7.8, East South Central households using AC, daytime with someone home: ≤69 °F 22.1%, 70 °F 20.7%, 71–73 °F 29.5%, 74–76 °F 19.5%, ≥77 °F 8.3% → median 71–73 °F (21.7–22.8 °C; shares computed from table counts). High value matches the 24–24.4 °C used in Stone et al. 2023 and Wijesuriya et al. 2024. Self-reported. Previous placeholder 23/24/25 °C.
column16: RECS 2020 East South Central survey (official statistic).

column12: Share of homes with working air conditioning (BLD-04). RECS 2020 Tennessee: 93% use AC (RSE 1.37%); East South Central 93.8%. Census LACE 2023 (experimental): Davidson County 97.7% (±0.1), Davidson tracts 89.7–100% (p10 94.9%). Low value covers the poorest tracts and window-unit-only homes. AHS has no Nashville metro sample. Previous placeholder 0.85/0.92/0.97.
column16: RECS 2020 Tennessee and Census LACE 2023 (experimental) for Davidson.

column12: Indoor air temperature above which a person-hour counts as indoor heat exposure. 26 °C: older adults, core temperature +0.2 °C at 26 °C vs +0.7 °C at 31 °C over 8 h (Meade et al. 2024); CIBSE TM59 bedroom limit. 28 °C: proposed U.S. maximum safe indoor temperature, still air, 50% RH (Huizenga et al. 2024 pp. 7–8); ASHRAE 55 upper limit. 32 °C: acute strain. WHO 2018 gives no numeric limit. Dry-bulb only; humid heat index is higher. Range unchanged; now sourced.
column16: Randomised trial (Meade 2024) and proposed U.S. limit (Huizenga 2024).

column12: Excess heat-illness ED visits per person-hour of indoor heat exposure. OLS of Davidson annual visits 2014–2023 (Tennessee Department of Health) on simulated indoor heat exposure without outages (pipeline.lineb calibrate): k = 4.34e-06 (SE 8.8e-07), R² 0.753, Spearman ρ 0.697 (p 0.025); range = k ± 1.96 SE. Ten annual points; exposure is simulated. Leave-one-year-out: Q² 0.659, mean absolute error 11.5%, k 4e-06–4.7e-06; without 2020: k 4.18e-06, R² 0.911.
column16: Reproducible fit of local T1 data (10 annual points).
